title: Week 4 · Lesson 9: Renal Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 4 — Lesson 9: Renal Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal: Interpret kidney dysfunction as a perfusion, intrinsic-tissue, or obstruction problem; connect renal physiology to volume, potassium, acid-base, medication safety, and emergency disposition.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain filtration, tubular regulation, eGFR/creatinine context, RAAS, and ADH.
  • Differentiate prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal AKI.
  • Connect CKD to volume overload, hyperkalemia, acidosis, anemia, and mineral-bone disease.
  • Recognize medication and hemodynamic contributors to AKI.
  • Identify renal emergencies.

Part 1 — Kidney Functions

Kidneys filter plasma, regulate sodium/water/electrolytes, excrete acid and waste, support blood pressure, produce erythropoietin, and participate in vitamin-D activation. Glomerulus = filtration; tubules = reabsorption, secretion, and fine-tuning.

Creatinine is a useful trend, not a complete diagnosis. Muscle mass, age, baseline function, volume status, and the rate of change matter; eGFR and clinical context are essential.

Part 2 — GFR and Renal Perfusion

Reduced effective circulating volume/perfusion → GFR ↓ → creatinine may rise. Renal blood flow and arteriolar tone matter. Volume loss, shock, heart failure, cirrhosis, sepsis, medications, and vascular disease can impair effective kidney perfusion.

Part 3 — RAAS, Aldosterone, and ADH

Renin release leads to angiotensin II, vasoconstriction, and aldosterone signaling. Aldosterone → sodium reabsorption + potassium secretion; water follows sodium. ADH primarily increases collecting-duct water reabsorption.

ACE inhibitors/ARBs can lower intraglomerular pressure and aldosterone signaling. They are often clinically beneficial, but kidney function and potassium must be reviewed in the relevant patient and hemodynamic context; do not stop or start them reflexively without assessment.

Part 4 — AKI: Three Questions

Prerenal: is perfusion inadequate? Think dehydration, hemorrhage, shock, over-diuresis, heart failure, cirrhosis, sepsis.

Intrinsic: is kidney tissue injured? Think tubular injury, glomerular disease, interstitial nephritis, vascular injury, nephrotoxins.

Postrenal: is urine flow obstructed? Think BPH, stones, pelvic malignancy, strictures, neurogenic retention, bilateral/solitary-kidney obstruction.

Assess history, medication exposures (including NSAIDs/diuretics/RAAS agents where relevant), volume/perfusion, urinalysis, trend, urine output, bladder/obstruction clues, and appropriate imaging/pathways.

Part 5 — Potassium and Acid–Base

Kidneys are central to potassium excretion and acid excretion/bicarbonate regulation. Reduced excretion, hypoaldosterone states, tissue breakdown, acidosis, and medications can contribute to hyperkalemia.

Severe hyperkalemia can cause lethal conduction abnormalities. ECG changes, weakness, significant renal dysfunction, or a concerning potassium result require urgent confirmation and emergency management pathway rather than outpatient observation.

Lungs regulate CO₂; kidneys regulate H⁺/HCO₃⁻. CKD can impair acid excretion and contribute to metabolic acidosis. Diarrhea can cause bicarbonate loss/metabolic acidosis; vomiting can cause acid loss/metabolic alkalosis.

Part 6 — CKD as a Multisystem Disease

Loss of nephron mass can produce volume overload, hypertension, hyperkalemia, acidosis, anemia from reduced erythropoietin, and mineral-bone abnormalities. Diabetes and hypertension are major contributors, while CKD also worsens cardiovascular risk and medication toxicity risk.

Part 7 — FNP Clinical Cases

A patient with vomiting/diarrhea, BP 92/58, dry mucosa, oliguria, and rising creatinine: volume depletion → renal perfusion ↓ → prerenal AKI is likely, but evaluate medication use, infection, bleeding, obstruction, and intrinsic injury.

An older patient with weak stream, distended bladder, oliguria, and rising creatinine: consider postrenal obstruction; obstruction requires timely evaluation.

A patient with CKD, weakness, markedly elevated potassium, and ECG changes: this is an emergency risk of arrhythmia, not routine laboratory follow-up.

FNP High-Yield Framework

AKI: perfusion, parenchyma, or plumbing.

RAAS: Ang II vasoconstriction; aldosterone sodium retention/potassium secretion; ADH water retention.

FNP decision: trend renal function, assess volume and obstruction, review medications, use urinalysis/targeted tests, and escalate for severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, shock, severe acidosis, uremic symptoms, or rapidly worsening renal function.
